description: Zero Day Con talks from Zero Day Con 2022.

talks.title: Panel Discussion - The Power of Collective Intelligence in Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Provides panel Discussion - The Power of Collective Intelligence in Cybersecurity and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Collective Intelligence in Practice

Panelists define collective intelligence as large groups sharing knowledge to solve complex problems in cybersecurity. They argue effective organizations break down silos between departments like HR, accounting, and security so diverse perspectives contribute to threat understanding and response.

Human and Machine Roles

Speakers emphasize augmenting—not replacing—human judgment with AI and automation. Pattern detection and noise filtering suit machines; gut feel and creative investigation still require experienced analysts. Soft skills such as communication and collaboration remain essential.

Organizational Barriers

Paul notes many firms struggle to deploy collective intelligence because distributed architectures, specialized pockets of expertise, and complexity stifle knowledge sharing. Several panelists call simplification a prerequisite for harnessing intelligence already present in the organization.

Talent and Retention

The discussion closes on hiring difficulty in cybersecurity, stressing retention and placing the right people in the right roles as part of making collective intelligence work.

talks.title: Panel Discussion - Zero Trust: From Digital Identity to Managing Supply Chain Risks
talks.teaser: Evaluates panel Discussion - Zero Trust: From Digital Identity to Managing Supply Chain Risks and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Defining Zero Trust

Panelists trace "zero trust" to Stephen Marsh's 1994 thesis, later popularized by Forrester and NIST as perimeterless security where every user, device, and service is untrusted by default—summarized as "never trust, always verify."

Real-World Flexibility

Speakers reject one-size-fits-all zero trust. Startups on uniform Microsoft stacks differ from heterogeneous enterprises with OT, manufacturing, and legacy apps. Controls must map to asset criticality or risk blocking legitimate work.

Graduated Assurance

Trust should scale like physical badges: lobby access differs from server-room biometrics. MFA is necessary but insufficient—users habitually approve prompts, machine integrations skip MFA entirely, and pilots carrying sensitive cargo need location and device pairing without crushing privacy.

Supply Chain and Identity

Discussion extends to digital identity, pilot device pairing at ASL, and supply-chain risk inside zero-trust programs, emphasizing visibility into users, data, devices, and applications before enforcing universal policies.

talks.title: Panel Discussion - The Great Debate on Cyberwarfare
talks.teaser: Reviews panel Discussion - The Great Debate on Cyberwarfare and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview:
At Zero Day Con, an expert panel featuring Brian Johnson, Donna Craven, Loukik Suther, and Pat Lordan convenes to debate the strategic, operational, and legal complexities of modern cyberwarfare and state-sponsored intrusions. Drawing from diverse backgrounds spanning military intelligence, national law enforcement, corrections critical infrastructure, and naval criminal investigation, the panelists analyze the blurred boundary separating financially motivated cybercrime from geopolitical warfare. The discussion centers on the collateral damage inflicted upon civilian infrastructure—highlighting Ireland's Health Service Executive (HSE) ransomware catastrophe—and evaluates the systemic hurdles hindering interagency cooperation, incident reporting, and cryptocurrency tracing.

Key Topics:
- Collateral damage and military proportionality in asymmetric cyber warfare
- The intersection of state-sponsored actors and cybercriminal syndicates (HSE Conti ransomware attack)
- Organizational barriers, under-reporting of incidents, and misplaced incident containment confidence
- Global law enforcement coordination (Garda Síochána, Interpol, Europol, NCIS) and FATF cryptocurrency regulation

Technical Details:
Brian Johnson opens by comparing kinetic military planning with cyber operations, emphasizing that conventional warfare requires precise targeting, weapon yields, and collateral damage estimates. In cyberspace, however, assessing proportionality and collateral damage is exponentially more difficult because malware operators cannot easily constrain network propagation or predict cascading dependencies across interconnected civilian systems. The panel examines the 2021 ransomware attack against Ireland's Health Service Executive (HSE) by the Conti group as a prime case study of civilian impact. The attackers maintained an eight-week dwell time inside the HSE environment before deploying ransomware, causing catastrophic disruptions to hospital appointments, surgeries, and clinical care. The panelists emphasize that whether an attack is executed for financial extortion or nation-state disruption, the operational result mirrors warfare against civilian populations, challenging conventional military doctrines of proportionality and attribution.

Loukik Suther and Pat Lordan address the attribution and investigative dilemmas inherent to cyber guerrilla warfare, where threat actors operate from distant, non-extradition jurisdictions using proxy infrastructure and distributed botnets. Lordan critiques the persistent issue of under-reporting and premature containment declarations, citing an enterprise incident where an organization lost €1 million in a business email compromise (BEC) and was hours away from losing another €7 million; within two hours of discovery, the company's IT leadership falsely claimed the intruders were 100% eradicated. The panelists stress that reporting incidents to national authorities (such as the Garda National Cyber Crime Bureau, NCIS, Europol, and Interpol) provides essential cross-sector telemetry that prevents subsequent attacks by identical threat groups. Addressing the financial infrastructure of modern cybercrime, Lordan highlights that proceeds from BEC, phishing, smishing, and fraud directly subsidize human trafficking, drug operations, and armed conflicts. While pointing to investigative breakthroughs in blockchain analysis—such as the FBI's recovery of ransom payments in the Colonial Pipeline incident—Lordan notes that asset recovery remains severely constrained once cryptocurrency flows into jurisdictions lacking Financial Action Task Force (FATF) compliance or mutual legal assistance treaties.

Key Takeaways:
Defenders across both public and private sectors must treat cybersecurity as a collaborative national security priority rather than an isolated IT discipline, actively sharing indicators of compromise (IOCs) with law enforcement to protect peer institutions. Critical infrastructure organizations must maintain rigorous incident response and threat hunting protocols, resisting the urge to declare containment prematurely without comprehensive forensic sweeps across long dwell-time environments. Governments and international bodies must enforce uniform anti-money laundering and know-your-customer (KYC) regulations across cryptocurrency exchanges following FATF standards to dismantle the financial rails funding cyber warfare and transnational organized crime.

talks.title: ZDC22: Seamus Lennon, Threatlocker
talks.teaser: Presents ZDC22: Seamus Lennon, Threatlocker and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview:
Seamus Lennon, a solutions engineer at ThreatLocker, presents an argument for replacing reactive endpoint detection with an operational Zero Trust architecture. Addressing the reality that modern malware and ransomware exfiltrate sensitive data and weaponize legitimate administration tools, Lennon highlights why traditional antivirus and threat hunting fail against zero-day threats. The presentation outlines the core principles of endpoint Zero Trust—application whitelisting, ringfencing, storage control, and elevation control—to neutralize living-off-the-land attacks and unauthorized software execution.

Key Topics:
- The limitations of reactive scanning and signature detection against zero-day ransomware
- Double extortion trends and living-off-the-land (LotL) execution tactics
- The Security Triangle framework: scanning, security awareness training, and operational controls
- Core Zero Trust endpoint controls: default-deny whitelisting, ringfencing, storage control, and elevation control

Technical Details:
Lennon highlights the massive scale of malicious software, noting that security solutions detect approximately 540,000 new malware samples daily among over a billion existing variants, with at least four businesses impacted by malware or ransomware every minute. Furthermore, the operational model of ransomware has shifted from simple on-disk encryption (such as WannaCry in 2014) to double extortion. Citing research from Coveware, Lennon notes that over 70% of modern ransomware attacks incorporate data exfiltration. Attackers routinely weaponize remote management tools (RMM) and living-off-the-land binaries (LotL) already present on victim endpoints. For instance, adversaries leverage PowerShell and the Windows command prompt (cmd.exe) to exfiltrate files over the network, or execute arbitrary payloads hosted on GitHub directly in protected memory using rundll32.exe to evade traditional file scanners.

To address the limitations of reactive antivirus engines that only recognize known malicious patterns, Lennon introduces the Security Triangle framework. While vulnerability scanning forms one side and user security awareness training forms another, organizational defense often breaks down on the third side: operational controls. Traditional training cannot prevent every user from clicking malicious links, making technical controls essential. ThreatLocker implements a default-deny zero-trust model where all unapproved executables, DLLs, and scripts are blocked by default, neutralizing zero-day execution.

Beyond application whitelisting, Lennon details ringfencing, which restricts how approved applications interact with operating system resources, files, and other binaries. Even if Microsoft Office is permitted, ringfencing policies strictly prevent Office processes from launching PowerShell, severing a primary initial delivery vector. Similarly, ringfencing blocks PowerShell from accessing local data stores or outbound network connections, stopping exfiltration. Storage control enforces application-specific access rules; for example, backup directories are restricted so that only designated backup software can access or modify backup archives, preventing ransomware operators from discovering and wiping backups to compel ransom payments. Finally, elevation control allows specific approved administrative tasks or applications to run with elevated privileges without granting users persistent local administrator rights.

Key Takeaways:
Organizations must transition from signature and heuristic detection to an endpoint Zero Trust model based on least privilege and default-deny policies. Deploying application whitelisting prevents unapproved zero-day binaries from executing, while ringfencing restricts trusted applications like Microsoft Office and PowerShell from interacting with each other, accessing sensitive file directories, or connecting to the internet. Additionally, critical backup repositories must be shielded with storage controls so only authorized backup utilities can modify them, and persistent local administrator rights should be replaced with controlled, on-demand application elevation.
